Working from Home: A Mixed Blessing

Over the past several years, remote work has shifted from a rare perk to an everyday arrangement for millions of employees. While this change brings real benefits, it also creates challenges that neither workers nor employers can afford to ignore.

The most obvious advantage is the time saved by eliminating the commute. An employee who once spent an hour each way in traffic gains back roughly ten hours a week, time that can go toward family, exercise, or rest. Remote work also offers flexibility, allowing people to arrange their day around their most productive hours or personal responsibilities, such as caring for children or elderly parents. For employers, the benefits include lower office costs and access to talent from a much wider geographic area, since hiring is no longer limited to people who live nearby.

However, working from home has significant drawbacks. Many people struggle with isolation, missing the casual conversations and sense of belonging that come from sharing a physical workplace. This can affect mental health and weaken team relationships over time. Collaboration may also suffer; spontaneous problem-solving and mentoring happen more naturally in person than over scheduled video calls, which can especially disadvantage younger employees who are still learning. Finally, the boundary between work and home can blur. When the office is the kitchen table, it becomes harder to switch off, and many remote workers report working longer hours rather than fewer.

In weighing these factors, it seems clear that remote work is neither a perfect solution nor a passing trend. Its value depends largely on the nature of the job and the personality of the worker. For many organizations, a hybrid model, combining the focus and flexibility of home with the connection of the office, may offer the best of both worlds. The challenge ahead is designing arrangements that keep the benefits while limiting the costs.

Whether Mercy is the right choice in a given match depends far more on team composition, game mode, and your own skill set than on the nationality of your teammates. Players from China, or from any other region, do not require a particular support hero. That said, there are some practical considerations worth examining when you are coordinating with teammates who may not share your first language.

**Strengths of Mercy in such situations**

Mercy is among the heroes least dependent on verbal coordination. Her core gameplay loop of sustaining a damaged ally, amplifying damage with her blue beam, and resurrecting fallen teammates is largely reactive. You respond to what you observe on screen rather than to callouts. The in-game ping system and communication wheel convey most of the information she needs, such as "I need healing" or "Enemy spotted," and these messages are automatically localized. This makes Mercy a reasonable option when language barriers limit voice communication.

Her Guardian Angel mobility also allows her to follow aggressive players closely. If your teammates favor a high-tempo, dive-oriented style, as is often seen on Asian servers, Mercy's ability to stay attached to a flanking Genji, Echo, or Pharah can be particularly valuable.

**Limitations to consider**

Mercy's raw healing output is modest compared with heroes such as Ana, Kiriko, or Baptiste, and she offers little in the way of crowd control or burst damage. In matches where the enemy team applies heavy pressure, or where your tanks require substantial sustain, she may struggle. Her resurrection is powerful but leaves her exposed, and experienced opponents will target her accordingly.

**Recommendation**

Mercy is a sound selection if your team has strong damage dealers who benefit from damage boost, if your partner support can provide more burst healing, and if communication is primarily non-verbal. If your team lacks reliable output or your tank is struggling, a hero with greater healing throughput or utility may be more effective.

Ultimately, the best approach is to observe your teammates' preferred heroes and playstyle during the first fight and adjust accordingly. Flexibility, rather than any single hero choice, is the most valuable contribution a support player can make.

Practical Skills or Theory at University?

Today many students go to university because they want a good job in the future. Because of this, people have different ideas about what universities should teach. Some people think universities must teach practical job skills, but other people believe theoretical knowledge is more important. In this essay I will discuss both side and give my own opinion.

On the one hand, practical skills are very useful. When students finish university, companies want them to start working quickly. If a student already know how to use computer programs, write reports or work in a team, the company don't need to train them for a long time. Also, many students pay a lot of money for university, so they want to learn things they can use in real life. For example, my cousin studied business, but he said he never learned how to make a simple budget in Excel. He had to learn it by himself after he got a job.

On the other hand, theoretical knowledge is also important. Theory helps students understand why things happen, not only how to do them. Technology changes very fast, so a skill that is useful today maybe will be old in five years. But if students understand the basic ideas, they can learn new skills more easy. For example, doctors and engineers need a strong theory background, because without it they can make dangerous mistakes.

In my opinion, universities should teach both, but theory should be the base. Students can learn some practical skills from internships or part-time jobs, and universities can help them to find these chances. However, deep knowledge is hard to get alone, so this is the main job of university.

In conclusion, both practical skills and theory have advantages. I think a good university gives students strong knowledge and also some chance to practice, so they are ready for work and for the future.

The parrot's name was Doctor, and he was older than the marriage.

Walt had bought him in 1979 from a man at a flea market who swore the bird could recite the Gettysburg Address. He couldn't. What he could do, within a month of coming home, was imitate Walt perfectly: the throat clear before a phone call, the low whistle when a pot boiled over, and above all, the sentence Walt shouted every single morning when he pulled open the kitchen curtains.

"Boy, its a joyous day outside!"

He said it in rain. He said it in sleet. He said it the February the furnace died and they wore coats to breakfast. June used to roll her eyes and tell him it was eight degrees and the sky looked like dishwater, and Walt would say that was precisely what made it joyous, that any fool could be happy in sunshine.

Doctor learned it in Walt's exact voice, gravel and all, and for forty-four years the two of them said it together, man and bird, while June buttered toast and pretended to be annoyed.

Walt died in March.

It was quick, which everyone told June was a mercy, and she supposed it was. The funeral was full. The casseroles came and went. Her daughter stayed for a week and then had to get back to Phoenix, and then the house was quiet in a way June had never heard it be quiet, a quiet with corners.

The first morning alone, she didn't open the curtains. She sat at the table in the dim kitchen with her coffee going cold and did not think about anything at all.

Behind her, Doctor shifted on his perch.

"Boy," he said, in Walt's voice, "its a joyous day outside!"

June dropped her cup.

She had forgotten. That was the stupid thing. In all the arrangements, the phone calls, the paperwork, she had forgotten the bird knew how to be him.

She did not open the curtains that day, or the next. But Doctor said it anyway, every morning at seven, bright and certain, as if nothing had happened. As if Walt were just in the other room. Sometimes June would answer before she could stop herself, "It's eight degrees, you old fool," and then she'd hear herself and have to sit down.

Her daughter suggested, gently, on the phone, that maybe the bird should go to someone else. A rescue. Somewhere with other parrots.

"He's fine," June said.

"Mom. Is he fine, or are you?"

June didn't answer that.

The truth was that she had started waiting for it. She woke at six forty-five and lay listening. She was afraid of the morning he wouldn't say it, and more afraid of the morning he would, because each time the voice came, for one half-second, her heart forgot. And then remembered. Every day it got to lose him again.

In May, on a morning when the light came through the gap in the curtains in a long gold bar across the linoleum, Doctor said it, and June stood up and walked to the window.

She pulled the curtains open.

It was, in fact, beautiful. The lilacs Walt had planted were blooming. A robin was working the lawn. The sky was the clean, rinsed blue that comes after a night of rain.

"Boy," Doctor said behind her, "its a joyous day outside."

"I know," June whispered. "I know it is."

She stood there a long time, letting the sun reach her, a joyous day that he would never see, and the bird kept saying it, in his voice, over and over, as if trying to teach her the words.

**Gunmen Kill at Least 23 at Tunisia's Bardo Museum**

TUNIS, Tunisia — At least 23 people were killed Wednesday when gunmen stormed the Bardo National Museum in the Tunisian capital, targeting one of the country's best-known cultural landmarks and the tourism industry on which its economy depends.

Most of the dead were foreign visitors, several of whom had come ashore earlier that day from cruise ships docked in Tunis. Security forces ended a standoff inside the museum by killing two of the attackers, and dozens of people were treated for injuries. The Bardo, which houses one of the world's great collections of Roman mosaics, sits next to the national parliament.

The attack has shaken a country often described as the one success story of the Arab Spring. Since the 2011 revolution that ousted President Zine El Abidine Ben Ali, Tunisia has adopted a new constitution and held free elections. Yet it has also become one of the largest sources of foreign fighters for extremist groups in Syria and Iraq, with an estimated 3,000 Tunisians believed to have joined them.

For Mabrouka M'Barek, a former member of Tunisia's National Constituent Assembly, those two facts are closely linked. In her view, Tunisia has failed to "recruit" its own citizens into society, leaving many young people, particularly in the country's poorer interior regions, feeling they have no stake in the new democracy. When the state offers them no place, she argues, extremist groups are eager to offer one instead.

Her argument shifts the focus beyond policing and toward unemployment, regional inequality and political exclusion, the same grievances that fueled the 2011 uprising.

Tunisian leaders have vowed a forceful response, and investigators are working to identify who planned the assault. But as the nation mourns, many Tunisians are asking whether their young democracy can reach its next generation before the recruiters do.

Working from home has become normal for many people, and it has both good and bad sides.

On the positive side, remote workers save time and money because they no longer have to commute. My mom, for example, used to spend over an hour driving every day, and now she uses that time to cook dinner and help me with homework. Working from home also gives people more flexibility to plan their own schedules.

On the other hand, there are real disadvantages. Many people feel lonely without coworkers around, and it can be harder to communicate with a team through screens. Another problem is that home is full of distractions, like television, pets, or family members, which can make it difficult to focus. Some people also find it hard to stop working when their office is in their bedroom.

Overall, working from home can be great, but only if people find ways to stay connected and set clear boundaries.

Reaching for the Stars Without Neglecting Home

Every year, governments spend billions on rockets, probes, and telescopes, while millions of people lack clean water, healthcare, or schooling. It is easy to see why critics argue that this money belongs on Earth. Yet treating space exploration and earthly problems as rivals misunderstands how both progress.

The case against space spending is emotionally powerful. A single Mars mission could fund hospitals or vaccination campaigns. When people suffer now, spending on distant planets can seem like a luxury for wealthy nations.

However, space budgets are smaller than many assume. NASA receives less than half a percent of the U.S. federal budget, a fraction of what goes to defense or health programs. More importantly, space research repays its cost in practical ways. Satellites track hurricanes, monitor crops, and measure climate change. Technologies first developed for spaceflight have led to improvements in water purification, medical imaging, and solar power. Space programs also inspire students to pursue science and engineering.

Governments should therefore continue funding space exploration, but wisely: prioritizing missions with clear scientific or social value and cooperating internationally to share costs. Looking upward, in the end, often helps us take better care of the ground beneath our feet.

Should Governments Fund Space Exploration?

Some people believe money spent on space exploration should go toward problems like poverty and disease. While these problems are serious, I believe governments should continue funding space exploration.

First, space research helps solve problems on Earth. Weather satellites warn people about storms, and GPS helps with everything from farming to emergency services. Many inventions, like better water filters and medical scanners, came from space programs.

Second, space exploration inspires young people. When students watch a rover land on Mars, many become interested in science and engineering, which leads to new discoveries.

Finally, space budgets are relatively small compared to other government spending, so cutting them would not end poverty.

In conclusion, space exploration and solving earthly problems are not opposites. By investing in space, governments also invest in a better future on Earth.

Product feeds on large e-commerce platforms interleave organic recommendations with sponsored items, and the placement of advertisements has traditionally been optimized for immediate advertising revenue. This short-term focus overlooks a significant side effect: poorly placed or excessive advertisements can depress user engagement with organic content, reducing long-term platform value. In this paper, we formulate advertising allocation in product feeds as a sequential decision-making problem whose objective is to maximize organic traffic while satisfying constraints on advertising exposure and revenue. We propose a reinforcement learning framework in which an agent determines, at each request, the number and positions of advertisements to insert into a feed, conditioned on user context and the candidate item list. To address the sparsity and delay of engagement signals, we design a reward that combines immediate click feedback with a learned estimate of downstream browsing depth, and we employ a constrained policy optimization scheme to enforce platform-level advertising targets. Offline evaluations on large-scale logged data and online A/B tests on a major e-commerce platform show that our method substantially increases organic clicks and session length while maintaining advertising revenue, outperforming fixed-slot and greedy allocation baselines.

The nematic phase of FeSe, which emerges near 90 K without accompanying long-range magnetic order, provides an ideal setting for isolating the electronic origin of rotational symmetry breaking in iron-based superconductors. Using high-resolution angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy on mechanically detwinned single crystals, we determine the momentum- and orbital-resolved evolution of the electronic structure across the nematic transition. We find that the d_xz/d_yz splitting at the Brillouin zone corner reaches approximately 50 meV at low temperature, establishing the characteristic nematic energy scale, while the splitting near the zone center is markedly smaller, indicating a strongly momentum-dependent order parameter. Strikingly, only one electron pocket is observed in the nematic state; the pocket expected at the Y point is absent within our experimental resolution. We discuss how orbital-selective correlations and the d_xy orbital contribute to this suppression, and argue that the resulting anisotropic Fermi surface naturally accounts for the highly anisotropic superconducting gap and the absence of magnetic order in FeSe.
